content: Terconazole is an antifungal medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of vulvovaginal candidiasis (moniliasis). Common adverse reactions include vulvovaginal burning, itching, headache, dysmenorrhea, abdominal pain, asthenia, influenza-like illness (fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, arthralgia, malaise), hypersensitivity reactions, anaphylaxis, facial edema, bronchospasm, rash, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and urticaria. For adult patients, the FDA-approved dosage involves intravaginal administration of one full applicator (5 g) of Terconazole Vaginal Cream (20 mg terconazole) once daily at bedtime for seven consecutive days, or one full applicator (5 g) of Terconazole Vaginal Cream (40 mg terconazole) once daily at bedtime for three consecutive days. Before prescribing another course of therapy, the diagnosis should be reconfirmed using smears and/or cultures, and other pathogens associated with vulvovaginitis should be ruled out. The therapeutic effect of Terconazole is not affected by menstruation. There is limited information regarding off-label use of Terconazole in both guideline-supported and non-guideline-supported contexts for adult patients. Similarly, there is limited information on FDA-labeled indications, dosage, and off-label use for pediatric patients. Terconazole is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to the drug or its components. Serious adverse reactions, such as anaphylaxis and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if these reactions occur. Adverse reactions observed in clinical trials include headache, vulvovaginal burning, itching, and irritation. The most common adverse reaction leading to discontinuation was vulvovaginal itching. Post-marketing reports have identified additional adverse reactions, including asthenia, influenza-like illness (fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, arthralgia, malaise), hypersensitivity reactions (anaphylaxis, facial edema), dizziness, bronchospasm, rash, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and urticaria. There is limited information on drug interactions with Terconazole. Regarding use in specific populations, there is no FDA guidance on its use during pregnancy, labor and delivery, nursing, pediatric, geriatric, or immunocompromised settings, nor in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Additionally, there is no specific guidance on its use in relation to gender or race. In cases of overdose, supportive and symptomatic measures should be implemented. If the cream is ingested orally, or accidentally applied to the eyes, appropriate measures such as rinsing with clean water or saline and seeking medical attention should be taken. Terconazole works by inhibiting fungal cytochrome P-450-mediated 14-alpha-lanosterol demethylase, an enzyme necessary for converting lanosterol to ergosterol, a key component of fungal cell membranes. This inhibition leads to the accumulation of 14-alpha-methyl sterols and a loss of ergosterol, which compromises the fungal cell wall. Mammalian cell demethylation is less sensitive to Terconazole inhibition. The drug exhibits antifungal activity in vitro against Candida albicans and other Candida species, while typically sparing beneficial Lactobacillus species found in the human vagina. Pharmacokinetically, following a single intravaginal application of a suppository containing 240 mg of Terconazole, approximately 70% of the drug remains in the vaginal area during the retention period (16 hours), and about 10% is systemically absorbed over seven days. Maximum plasma concentrations occur 5 to 10 hours after intravaginal application. Systemic exposure is proportional to the applied dose, and the drug is extensively metabolized (>95%). There is no significant increase in plasma concentration or overall exposure after multiple daily applications. Patients should use Terconazole as prescribed, even if symptoms improve quickly. Sexual intercourse should be avoided if advised by a physician. Partners experiencing penile itching, redness, or discomfort should consult a physician. The medication can be used during menstruation, but tampons should be avoided as they may absorb the medication. External pads or napkins are recommended. Patients should maintain a dry genital area, avoid douching unless directed by a physician, and refrain from scratching to prevent further irritation or infection spread. Discuss any concurrent medications with a physician, as some drugs may increase susceptibility to infection. A nutritious diet is also recommended to support general health. There is no established interaction between alcohol and Terconazole, but patients should consult their physician regarding alcohol use while on this medication. The brand name for Terconazole is TERCONAZOLE®. There is limited information on look-alike drug names for Terconazole.
